issues.legal_issue: The presumption of a lost grant is unavailable when acceptable evidence establishes the terms of the grant.
material_facts: The trustees produced extracts from the inam register and statements made during the inam inquiry concerning the temple lands.
The Court found that the records clearly established the terms of the grants to the deities.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of lost grant could not be invoked because acceptable evidence of the terms of the grants was available.
issues.legal_principle: A lost grant may be presumed to support long and quiet possession when actual evidence of title or the grant’s terms is unavailable. It cannot be presumed where sufficient and convincing evidence establishes the grant’s nature and the person to whom it was made. The Court relied on Sankaranarayana Pillayan v. H.R.E. Board, Madras; Buddu Satyanarayana v. Konduru Venkatapayya; Maginiram Sitaram v. Kasturbai Manibhai; and Mohamed Muzafar Ali Musavi v. Jabeda Khatun.

predicates.temple_endowment_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over title to property granted for a temple endowment.
predicates.reliable_evidence_of_grant_terms: The parties produced acceptable records that establish the terms of the original grant.

issues.definition: When a temple-endowment title dispute is supported by reliable evidence of the grant’s terms, the lost-grant presumption is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A grant shown by reliable records to comprise the land for a deity vests both interests in the land in the deity, rather than in the archakas managing or enjoying it.
material_facts: The inam records described the land as granted to the deity for the temple and confirmed the grant to the temple.
The records identified an archaka as the person managing or enjoying the land, while also recording that its produce or income was used for the deity’s services.

The archakas and their predecessors possessed and dealt with the land, but their documents and conduct were consistent with their possession in their capacity as archakas and de facto trustees; they did not establish an independent title to the land.
issues.conclusion: The grants comprised both the melvaram and kudivaram interests, and the archakas could not claim title contrary to the deity’s ownership on the basis of their possession or alienations.
issues.legal_principle: The entries in an inam register are important evidence of the nature and extent of a grant, particularly where direct evidence is unavailable; an inam statement may be considered with the register, but the register’s recitals carry greater evidentiary weight. Long enjoyment does not establish a different grant where reliable records establish its terms. Possession by an archaka as manager or de facto trustee does not confer a personal interest that can be asserted against the deity. The Court relied on Arunachalam Chetti v. Venkata Chalapathi Guruswamigal; Secretary of State for India v. Vidhya Thirta Swamigal; Buddu Satyanarayana v. Konduru Venkatapayya; and Narayanamurthi v. Achaya Sastrulu.

predicates.temple_endowment_title_suit: The proceeding concerns title to land claimed as a temple endowment.
predicates.official_grant_records_identify_deity_as: Official grant records identify the deity or temple as the grantee of the property.
predicates.records_describe_land_as_granted: The records describe the land itself as the subject of the grant, rather than only a revenue interest in it.
predicates.archaka_possession_is_for_temple_managem: The archaka’s possession and enjoyment of the land are shown as connected to managing the temple and providing for its services.

issues.definition: Where official records in a temple-endowment title suit identify the deity as grantee of the land and the archaka’s possession is for temple management, both interests in the land belong to the deity.

issues.legal_issue: A court in an ejectment suit based on established title cannot allocate temple land to an archaka as remuneration without a basis in the pleadings or evidence.
material_facts: The trustees brought suits for ejectment and recovery of temple properties, and the courts found that title to the properties was in the deities.
The High Court nevertheless directed that half of the lands be allotted to the archakas as remuneration.
There was no pleading or evidence supporting that apportionment; determining a proper allocation would depend on matters such as income, worship expenses, and reasonable remuneration.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in allocating land to the archakas in the ejectment suits; possession had to be delivered to the trustees who established title. Such provision for an archaka may be considered in an appropriate proceeding to frame a temple scheme, but not in these ejectment suits.
issues.legal_principle: In an ejectment suit, once the plaintiff establishes title and the defendant establishes no right to remain in possession, the court must award possession to the titleholder. Questions about providing remuneration or allocating temple property to an archaka are out of place without a proper basis in the pleadings and evidence; they may be considered in an appropriate temple-scheme proceeding. The Court relied on Buddu Satyanarayana v. Konduru Venkatapayya and referred to Brahmayya v. Rajaswaraswami Temple and Venkatadri v. Seshacharlu.

predicates.ejectment_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking ejectment and possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_establishes_title: The plaintiff establishes title to the property and the defendant does not establish a right to remain in possession.
predicates.no_pleading_or_evidence_supports_allocat: The pleadings and evidence provide no basis for allocating part of the property to the defendant as remuneration.

issues.definition: In an ejectment suit, when the plaintiff proves title and there is no pleaded or evidentiary basis for an allocation, possession goes to the titleholder without allocating land to the archaka.
